title: The sixth's colours blessed at Cnoc bheag
summary: At first light on the quay steps at Cnoc bheag the sixth regiment's new colours are blessed on an old staff kept in the Hawk house's own keeping, the whole ceremony held to the tide's own time and not the muster's, the regiment's clerk noting only that the priest would not be hurried for a schedule's sake.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh watches the camp from her garden wall
summary: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, retired at Àth dhìreach, watches the second regiment's camp rise from her own garden wall and is asked by its young captain whether the wall marks ground his picket line needs; it does not. She notes the town gives the company no trouble and is given none.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh writes to Sìleas nic Rath of the camp
summary: Beathag writes to Sìleas nic Rath that she trusts her own eyes on a garden wall better than she ever let herself trust the reports that once reached her desk from towns she had never stood in. The line is struck through once and left to stand, the ink thin enough to read beneath it.

title: The fourth marches down to the river
summary: The fourth regiment marches from Caol bheag to the river on a frosted morning, the whole town turned out along the road. Corporal Dùghall mac Iain's own mother stands at the mill corner and says nothing at all as he passes, which he takes, without either of them saying it, for the greater kindness.

title: The fourth's voyage down the Abhainn ghorm
summary: The fourth regiment goes down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar in refitted coal barges, the two days' journey the maps had promised done in a day and a half on the autumn spate, the barge-men steering more than rowing, the men passing the crossing in games, arguments and a harvest song none of them had thought to sing.

title: The hired hulls put out from Ros chiar
summary: The fourth regiment's hired dubhan hulls put out from Ros chiar into a turning sea, five days round the north cape with the tanks below decks giving off a smell that does not leave the men's kit for weeks. A boy of the second company goes overboard reaching for a loosed line and is hauled back half-drowned.

title: One hull parts company off the north cape
summary: In the worst of the second night's weather one of the fourth regiment's hired hulls is separated from the rest, puts into a cove on the far side of the north cape, and loses two days finding the others again, reaching Ceann mhòr three days behind the rest with crew and cargo whole.

title: The maor of Ceann mhòr gives up his house
summary: The maor of Ceann mhòr gives up the greater part of the old human magistrate's house to the fourth regiment without complaint, moving his own household into its two upper rooms, and takes afterwards to walking their narrow gallery of an evening remarking to whichever officer passes below that the army has undone in a fortnight what forty winters of sea air had not.

title: The maor's clerk keeps the two tongues apart
summary: The maor of Ceann mhòr's clerk, a Tuathaich woman of long service, addresses the fourth regiment's captain in Dia-thìris without a stumble and her own townsfolk, on the office's business, in the humans' tongue alone, the two tongues kept, in her own ordering of things, for two entirely different kinds of transaction.

title: Martha Greaves's letter reaches the magistrate's house
summary: Martha Greaves's single sheet asking that the fourth regiment be lodged at its own charge and not the town's is carried up the coast road and read aloud by the fourth's own captain to his assembled company. It is received and forwarded; the Board's late reply says only that the arrangement stands until the campaign's needs change it.

title: The Cathair gheal petition folded into a barrel of cod
summary: The fishermen of Cathair gheal draw up their petition on the quay before the boats go out, setting down only the days the searching has run and the hours a boat is commonly held, and send it to Caol mhòr folded inside a barrel of salt cod consigned, quite genuinely, to the Moot's own stores.

title: Dùghall hears the petition told as a soldier's tale
summary: A corporal of the second fleet, billeted a night at Ceann mhòr, tells Dùghall mac Iain the tale of the fish-barrel petition over their shared supper as dry entertainment and nothing graver, a story a searching soldier keeps by him for its comedy rather than its weight.

title: Dùghall billeted on Barabal of Ceann mhòr
summary: Once the magistrate's house is full past stretching, the maor's clerk billets Corporal Dùghall mac Iain on a widow of the town named Barabal, who keeps a loom in the room behind her kitchen; she opens her door to him with no more welcome than the clerk's own list had shown in its writing.

title: The tongue Barabal will not give him
summary: Barabal answers Corporal Dùghall mac Iain readily in Dia-thìris on the house's own business, but gives him, try as he may, not one word of the humans' tongue, though he hears her speak it easily across the yard wall to a neighbour; he comes to understand it a door shut on him alone.
